en: Having first prostrated at the lotus-feet of the Omniscient One, we [compose] this *Sarvajñasiddhi* for the sake of establishing the existence of the Omniscient One.
One folio is missing from the MS; an error occurred during the photographing of the manuscript.

Whatever statement is consistent with valid cognition and expresses a determined object is preceded, either directly or indirectly, by a cognition that has directly perceived that object—for example, the statement "fire is a burner."
This statement, "all conditioned phenomena are momentary," which expresses an object established by valid cognition, is in fact a *kāryahetu* (effect-reason);
its lack of proof (*asiddhi*) does not apply, because this statement possesses a true meaning due to the demonstration that all entities undergo momentary destruction.
Nor is there a contradiction, because [the reason] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);

nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even though speech in general may be preceded by doubt or error, speech whose object is ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— whether directly or indirectly— is necessarily preceded by a cognition that directly perceives that object,
otherwise it would be impossible for it to invariably accord with a means of valid cognition.
However, for people such as ourselves, an inference that establishes momentary destruction does not arise [directly],
nor does there exist a perception whose object is that [momentary destruction];
nevertheless, since that [inference] arises by way of the instruction of a person who has perceived it through direct perception, it is indeed preceded by perception through a traditional lineage.
This proof is supplemented by R 31.13–21.
The *Madhyamakaśāstra* (MS) begins after the lacuna with the word *yogāt*, which is also the last word cited by Ratnakīrti.
Since the MS text presupposes this proof both in terms of content and logical progression, it is reasonable to assume that the missing folio contained the aforementioned proof cited by Ratnakīrti.

If it is asked: "How can this [inference], which has a pervasion established by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) and whose production depends upon the probans (*sādhana*), be preceded by the instruction of another?"— [the answer is that] one must read "non-existence of a means of valid cognition" (*ṇābhāvasi°*) instead of "subverting means of valid cognition" (*ṇabādhakapramāṇa*).
If there were no instruction from another, the doubt itself—whether [the object] is established as momentary or non-momentary—would not arise;

and in the absence of this doubt, the means of proof would not function. [Objection: Surely, even without the instruction of another, who could prevent the arising of doubt caused by the grounds for error?

For even when an inference has arisen through a sign (*nimitta*), the determination that "this is that very same thing"— which occurs due to the mental confusion of a person of dull intellect who is deceived by the perception of successive similar [moments]— does not cease;
how could such doubt regarding what is not the reality arise or come into being without the instruction of another?
"Neither MS [is] appropriate" would be preferable.
Let there be doubt due to the instruction of another.
But how is it that [this knowledge] belongs only to one who perceives directly?
For surely, even for an inferer, this [knowledge] arising from instruction is entirely possible.
Indeed, it must be explained: from what does the doubt arise for that inferer which serves as the cause for the emergence of his inference?
If it is argued that this is because of the instruction on another means of inference, we say no,
because this same objection applies equally there as well.
If it is argued that there is no fault because each subsequent inferent’s doubt is preceded by the instruction of an inference from a prior proponent who is beginningless, we say no.

For all [inferents] are bound by ignorance (*avidyā*), and since this cause of doubt—consisting of a continuous succession of similar successive perceptions—is common to all, there is no room for such a doubt regarding the reason for inference when the mind is not opposed to its own contradictory error; thus, the status of being an inferent is untenable.

For if there were some direct perceiver who could act as a teacher, then others might become inferential knowers based on the instruction given by that teacher; however, in the absence of such a person who has directly perceived [the truth], inference cannot arise because there is no convention, since there is no manifestation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of non-erroneous knowledge in a knower. How, then, can one be called an inferential knower?
Therefore, a direct witness and teacher must be accepted;

and he who is the direct perceiver of all phenomena, such as their momentariness, and is the teacher, is the Blessed One, the crest-jewel of gods and demons, the omniscient one— thus [is it] free from darkness.

Having performed this for the sake of the All-Knowing One, whatever merit has been acquired by me,
by this may the entire world attain the state of omniscience.
The Proof of Omniscience by Paṇḍita Jitāri.
